dimension_1_problem_framing.text: The paper addresses the problem of predicting low stock prices for Tanzanian banks, emphasizing the economic importance of accurate stock price prediction for investments in developing countries like Tanzania and the particular difficulty posed by dynamic, volatile markets affected by geopolitical factors, as well as the inadequacy of traditional statistical and econometric methods for non-stationary financial time series. The study formulates this as a supervised prediction task on CRDB and NMB stock time series, comparing classical neural and regression models with a variational quantum neural network.

dimension_2_quantum_method.text: The quantum approach is a variational quantum neural network (VQNN), described as a quantum circuit learning model built as an ML algorithm for quantum computers that encodes classical stock data x into n-qubit quantum states |Ψ⟩ and processes them via a parametrized quantum circuit. The circuit uses Hadamard and CNOT gates as core components, is trained with a very small setting (learning rate 0.001, epoch 1, batch size 1), and is implemented on a simulator (PennyLane) where measurement outputs are converted back to classical predictions; the authors attribute potential learning acceleration to quantum superposition and entanglement.

dimension_3_key_results.text: Across performance metrics, the authors report mixed results: the VQNN shows the best RMSE and lowest MAE among the compared networks, which they attribute to strong resistance to overfitting, but it is outperformed by LSTM and MLR on MAPE and R², indicating those classical models better capture the variance and relative error structure of the stock prices. Visual comparisons for both CRDB and NMB show that all models can track the general trend of low stock prices, with MLR providing the closest overlap with actual prices; the authors note that VQNN performance is weaker on the more volatile NMB dataset than on CRDB.

dimension_4_classical_comparison.text: The study directly compares VQNN with classical LSTM, MLR, and a previously studied MLS-LSTM, finding that LSTM and MLR generally outperform both MLS-LSTM and VQNN on MAPE and R², and that the proposed classical models are more accurate than the prior MLS-LSTM baseline. While VQNN demonstrates favorable RMSE and MAE, the authors conclude overall that MLR and LSTM are more accurate and more consistent in predicting low stock prices for CRDB and NMB, and visually MLR best matches observed trends for both stocks.

dimension_5_stated_limitations.text: The authors acknowledge that the VQNN model suffers from overfitting when trained on the relatively large stock datasets used, leading to inconsistency and lower efficiency across performance indices despite its fast learning and small number of hidden neurons. They further note that VQNN prediction quality degrades on the more volatile NMB dataset, implying sensitivity to volatility, and in their recommendations they implicitly recognize limitations of the current setup by calling for broader datasets, richer input–output parameterizations, and more advanced VQC tuning and optimization methods.

dimension_6_future_work.text: For future work, the authors propose analyzing additional and more diverse stock datasets with varied input and output parameters, integrating evolutionary algorithms and hyper-tuned variational quantum circuits to improve both speed and accuracy of quantum models. They also recommend incorporating fundamental and sentiment analysis features, reflecting public opinion and company fundamentals, into future prediction models to better capture drivers of stock performance.

dimension_7_novelty_claim.text: The paper positions its contribution as a comparative analysis of classical (LSTM, MLR, MLS-LSTM) and quantum (VQNN) neural networks for low stock price prediction on Tanzanian bank data, improving prior LSTM-based work by adding dropout and more hidden layers, expanding MLR input dimensionality, and introducing a VQNN architecture based on variational quantum circuits. The authors claim that their proposed classical models achieve higher accuracy than previously reported MLS-LSTM baselines and that the VQNN demonstrates the ability to learn stock price trends quickly with fewer hidden neurons, albeit with noted limitations.

dimension_8_methodological_notes.text: Methodologically, the study uses real market data from the Dar Es Salaam Stock Exchange for CRDB and NMB, with 2,525 data points per stock, cleans missing trading days for consistency, and applies MinMax scaling to normalize features to [0,1], followed by an 80/20 train–test split. The LSTM is implemented as an eight-layer architecture with ReLU activation, dropout to mitigate overfitting, a time step of 105, and batch size and epoch both set to 100 and 105 respectively; the MLR network uses four stock datasets as inputs, a dense hidden layer with 100 neurons, ReLU activation, auto batch size, fixed random state, and up to 2,000 iterations. The VQNN encodes classical data into qubits and employs Hadamard and CNOT gates but is trained with very minimal hyperparameters (learning rate 0.001, epoch 1, batch size 1), and all models are evaluated with clearly defined metrics (MSE, MAE, MAPE, R², RMSE), which enhances interpretability but the sparse description of quantum resource requirements and extremely short VQNN training may limit reproducibility and the robustness of quantum–classical comparisons.

dimension_9_miscellaneous.text: The authors provide general conceptual framing of neural networks as ML approaches analogous to the human brain and highlight LSTM’s suitability for capturing long-term dependencies in stock data. They also discuss the broader shift from traditional statistical methods to ML and DL in stock prediction and reference prior applications of quantum methods in finance, such as quantum-based value-at-risk and expected shortfall prediction for ASEAN stock exchanges, to position their work in the emerging quantum finance literature.
